title: Chaff and grain of the cybercrime law
primary_topics: Constitutional analysis of the Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175) -- separating the constitutionally acceptable provisions from the potentially unconstitutional content-related offenses
The evolution of free expression from speech and press to Internet and social media as a constitutional mandate
The SC TRO on RA 10175 and CJ prediction that the Court will separate the chaff from the grain
sub_topics: RA 10175 three categories: (a) confidentiality/integrity/availability violations (hacking, illegal access, interception, data interference, cyber squatting); (b) computer-related offenses (forgery, fraud, identity theft); (c) content-related offenses (cybersex, child pornography, unsolicited communications, libel)
Categories (a) and (b) are constitutionally unremarkable -- legitimate state interests in protecting computers and identities
Category (c) content-related offenses creates a chilling effect that could be unconstitutional
Only senator who voted against RA 10175: Teofisto Guingona III
SC TRO: ex parte, effective immediately, 120 days; oral argument Jan. 15, 2013
Evolution of free expression: free speech, printing press, labor strikes, radio/TV/cinema, exit polls (ABS-CBN v. Comelec, Jan. 28, 2000), Internet/Twitter/Facebook
Internet: no previous restraint required -- like no permit needed to speak at gatherings or publish books
Time/place/manner restrictions permissible; content suppression (tax on excess circulation or excess emails) unconstitutional
Freedom of expression not absolute: lewd, obscene, seditious, libelous words subject to police power via clear and present danger test
Holmes fire-in-crowded-theater illustration: falsely shouting fire in a theater creates liability; same in open field does not
signature_phrases: digs deep into one of the most revered rights in a democracy--the right to free expression
the chilling effect of this provision could make it unconstitutional
Internet and its derivatives, like Twitter and Facebook, are also technological expansion of freedom of expression
a netizen can freely send and receive communications over cyberspace without previous restraint or censorship
the Supreme Court will separate the chaff from the grain in protecting cyberspace communications via the crucibles of freedom of expression
falsely shouting fire, fire in a crowded theater
If these words were shouted in an open field, there would be no liability because there is no clear and present danger

people: Sen. Teofisto Guingona III (only senator who voted against RA 10175)
Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes (clear and present danger test inventor)
cases: ABS-CBN v. Comelec (Jan. 28, 2000) -- exit polls as free expression
SC TRO on RA 10175 (ex parte, 120 days, oral argument Jan. 15, 2013)
laws_treaties: Republic Act No. 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012)

stances.claim: Categories (a) and (b) of RA 10175 are constitutionally unremarkable and serve legitimate state interests -- the grain.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-grain-identification before critiquing the problematic provisions

stances.claim: Category (c) content-related offenses create a chilling effect that could be unconstitutional because Internet communications are a technological expansion of free expression requiring the same protection from previous restraint and subsequent punishment.

A netizen should be able to send and receive communications without previous restraint, just as no one needs a permit to speak at a gathering or publish a book; only time/place/manner restrictions (not content suppression) are permissible.
stances.rhetorical_move: permit-analogy for Internet communications (no prior restraint)

stances.claim: The SC will correctly separate the chaff (content-related offenses with chilling effects) from the grain (legitimate cybercrime provisions) via the crucibles of freedom of expression.

notable_anecdotes: Holmes fire-in-crowded-theater illustration of the clear and present danger test -- contrasted with the same words in an open field producing no liability -- the column most memorable analogy.
CJ tracing of free expression technological evolution -- from speech and printing press to labor strikes, radio/TV/cinema, exit polls (ABS-CBN v. Comelec), and now Internet/Twitter/Facebook.

The tax-on-excess-circulation analogy: a tax on publication exceeding 50,000 circulation violates press freedom; a tax on more than 100 emails a day would be unconstitutional -- the clearest illustration of why content-restrictive Internet regulations are unconstitutional.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175), which the SC enjoined via an ex parte TRO (effective immediately for 120 days) after multiple petitioners -- including the only senator who voted against it, Teofisto Guingona III -- challenged its constitutionality, with oral argument set for January 15, 2013. He sorts the law's three categories: (a) confidentiality/integrity/availability violations (hacking, illegal access, interception, data interference, cyber squatting) and (b) computer-related offenses (forgery, fraud, identity theft) are constitutionally unremarkable -- the 'grain.' But (c) content-related offenses (cybersex, child pornography, unsolicited communications, and online libel) create a 'chilling effect' -- the 'chaff.' He argues that Internet and social media communications are a technological expansion of free expression in the same lineage as the printing press, radio/TV/cinema, and exit polls (ABS-CBN v. Comelec, 2000) -- requiring the same protection from previous restraint and subsequent punishment. A netizen needs no permit to communicate online, just as no one needs a permit to speak at a gathering or publish a book; local-government-style time/place/manner regulations are permissible but content suppression (like a tax on excess email volume) is not. Free expression is not absolute -- lewd, obscene, seditious, and libelous expression remains subject to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes' clear-and-present-danger test (falsely shouting 'fire' in a crowded theater creates liability; the same words in an open field do not). CJ predicts the SC will separate the chaff from the grain via the crucibles of freedom of expression.
